https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The Sweden Democrats leader, Jimmie Åkesson, delivers a speech at the party’s election results event near Stockholm after the far-right party slipped to third place. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Sweden Democrats leader, Jimmie Åkesson, delivers a speech at the party’s election results event near Stockholm after the far-right party slipped to third place. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images Sweden Analysis The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent The Sweden Democrats slipped to third after decades of growth, but their hardline positions have already reshaped the political mainstream Swedish centre-left opposition widens lead to three seats with 95% of votes counted – live Mon 14 Sep 2026 08.19 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.16 EDT Share Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable. In 2022, the party capitalised on electoral gains – and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration – and almost made its way into government . A supporting role in prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tidö coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment. This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs but serious political heavyweights. Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions. But Sunday’s results suggest the march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted – for now. Having fallen from Sweden’s second biggest party to third place and, with the right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appears to have lost its route into government. “What we saw yesterday [Sunday] was a historic setback for the Sweden Democrats,” says Niclas Nilsson, a lecturer and researcher at the anti-racism foundation Expo. “The party has grown in every government election since 1988.” The SD’s leader, Jimmie Åkesson, appeared visibly shocked when he addressed supporters late on election night. He said it was obvious they had lost some percentage points, but claimed they were still “winners”. He appeared to suggest his decision to be a team player and support coalition partner the Liberals may have played a role in their loss of support. View image in fullscreen Åkesson appeared visibly shocked by the Sweden Democrats’ setback at a party election-night event. Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty Images It is perhaps too soon to say why the party shed votes, said Nilsson, but some of its supporters may have gone to the Moderates, who had a good night. Another factor may have been that, after four years closely involved with the government, the SD is no longer able to claim it is an anti-establishment party. Turnout was about 80%, comparatively low for Sweden, which may also have played a role. There is also the fact that much of what the SD stand for has now become part of the Swedish political norm : anti-immigration, harsh approaches to crime and punishment, an attitude to integration that puts the onus on people moving to Sweden to abandon their culture and religion to adapt to “Swedish” norms. Their influence has spread to the centre-left Social Democrats who – after losing the last election – shifted their crime, immigration and integration strategies to the right. If the Moderates end up joining a coalition government with the Social Democrats, then the SD will be the biggest party in opposition, meaning it will still have a prominent role on the national stage. But if the Social Democrats are able to form a government without the Moderates, then the SD will again be on the outside looking in, which could help steer national conversation, politics and societal norms away from the right. View image in fullscreen Magdalena Andersson, the leader of the centre-left Social Democratic party, oversaw a rise in support by shifting to the right. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters How it responds to this moment will be key – to the party’s survival and the tenor of Swedish politics. But if, with no centre-right parties to answer to, they end up going further right to reinvigorate their base, it could have consequences in the future – and bring Swedish politics to new lows, Nilsson warned. After all, there is no shortage of far-right support in Sweden. Recruitment, the spread of ideas and mobilisation by far-right groups known as active clubs continue to grow without regulation or political rules – regardless of what is going on in Sweden’s parliament. https://nineoclock.ro/nicusor-dan-meets-.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Romania’s President Nicușor Dan Receives Foreign Ambassadors for the Presentation of Their Letters of Credence BUCHAREST — President Nicușor Dan received 18 newly appointed ambassadors at Cotroceni Palace on Friday, September 4, for the presentation of their letters of credence, with discussions ranging from Black Sea security and the war in Ukraine to defence, energy, trade, investment and Romania’s strategic partnerships. The ambassadors represent countries from Europe, Asia, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas, underlining the broad diplomatic agenda of the Romanian presidency and Bucharest’s interest in strengthening bilateral relations across several regions. The President welcomed the new ambassadors and wished them success in carrying out their mandates, assuring them of the full support of the Romanian authorities. Among the diplomats received by President Nicușor Dan were the ambassadors-designate of Vietnam, Saudi Arabia, Iran, the Republic of Korea, Serbia, Algeria, Denmark, Chile, Kazakhstan, Canada, Thailand, Côte d’Ivoire, Panama, Cambodia, Guatemala, El Salvador and Ghana. Vietnam: trade, investment and education During his meeting with Vietnam’s Ambassador-designate Le Vinh Thang , President Nicușor Dan welcomed the dynamic bilateral relationship and underlined Vietnam’s importance as a traditional economic and trade partner of Romania. The Vietnamese ambassador thanked Romania for the support provided to Vietnam during the COVID-19 pandemic. The two sides highlighted the positive development of bilateral dialogue, including at the highest level, as well as expanding sectoral cooperation in agriculture, trade, investment, labour, tourism, education and culture. Saudi Arabia: energy, defence and food security During his meeting with Saudi Ambassador-designate Khalid bin Eid Al-Shammari , President Nicușor Dan highlighted Saudi Arabia’s role as a key partner for Romania in the Middle East and the Gulf region. Both sides expressed interest in giving a new impetus to bilateral relations and welcomed the strong political dialogue between the two countries. The discussions focused particularly on expanding economic cooperation and strategic collaboration in energy, agriculture and food security, defence and internal affairs . Iran: call for diplomatic solutions In talks with Iran’s Ambassador-designate Seyed Mohsen Emadi , President Nicușor Dan referred to the traditional bilateral relationship between Romania and Iran. The two sides reiterated the importance of identifying a diplomatic solution to the conflict in the region , with the aim of reducing tensions and strengthening regional stability. South Korea: defence, nuclear energy and infrastructure The meeting with South Korea’s Ambassador-designate Hur Seung-chul focused on the strong Strategic Partnership between Romania and the Republic of Korea. President Nicușor Dan and the South Korean ambassador highlighted the excellent cooperation between the two countries in defence, civilian nuclear energy and infrastructure . They also expressed interest in strengthening economic relations through increased trade and investment and by diversifying sectoral cooperation. South Korea’s Ambassador-designate Hur Seung-chul Serbia: major connectivity projects During talks with Serbian Ambassador-designate Dragan Simeunović , the two sides focused on the friendly relationship between Romania and Serbia and the positive development of political dialogue. A key subject was the advancement of major connectivity projects in transport and energy , including the Timișoara–Belgrade motorway and the Arad–Mokrin gas pipeline . The role of the Romanian minority in Serbia and the Serbian minority in Romania was also highlighted as an important element in bringing the two countries closer together. Algeria: renewed political and economic cooperation President Nicușor Dan expressed Romania’s interest in revitalising political and diplomatic dialogue with Algeria during his meeting with Ambassador-designate Chaouki Chemmam . The two sides discussed expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest, including security and defence, energy, education and food security . The Romanian President also welcomed the continued interest of Algerian students in pursuing university studies in Romania, highlighting the long-standing educational ties between the two countries. Denmark: Black Sea security and NATO’s Eastern Flank Security was at the centre of President Nicușor Dan’s discussions with Denmark’s Ambassador-designate Stig Paolo Piras . The two sides discussed security in the Black Sea and the consequences of Russia’s war against Ukraine , while reaffirming their shared assessment of the security of NATO’s Eastern Flank and the main threats facing Europe and the Alliance. They also encouraged closer cooperation between chambers of commerce and business associations, as well as stronger investment and energy cooperation. The EU enlargement process was another topic on the agenda. President Nicușor Dan underlined Romania’s strong support for the European path of the Republic of Moldova, alongside that of the other candidate countries. Chile: a century of diplomatic relations During his meeting with Chilean Ambassador-designate Alex Wetzig Abdale , President Nicușor Dan highlighted the traditional friendship between Romania and Chile, strengthened over a century of diplomatic relations. Chile was described as one of Romania’s important partners in Latin America. The Romanian President expressed interest in deepening bilateral ties through increased trade and investment and expanding cooperation in cybersecurity, connectivity, agriculture, culture, research and education . Kazakhstan: expanding economic ties Talks with Kazakhstan’s Ambassador-designate Amangeldy Sainov highlighted the positive development of bilateral relations and the constructive political and diplomatic dialogue between Bucharest and Astana. Both sides underlined the significant potential for developing economic cooperation by encouraging investment and diversifying trade. The Romanian side also welcomed Kazakhstan’s principled position regarding respect by all states for the principles of international law. Canada: security, energy and support for Ukraine President Nicușor Dan and Canadian Ambassador-designate Kevin Rex welcomed the excellent level of bilateral relations and their shared views on key international issues. Their discussions covered NATO efficiency, energy security, continued support for Ukraine and the importance of multilateral cooperation. The two sides also discussed priorities under the Enhanced Partnership between Romania and Canada . Security cooperation was an important element of the meeting, including Canada’s participation in activities of the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group , cooperation on nuclear energy projects at Cernavodă , and the establishment of the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank . Thailand: technology and cybersecurity During talks with Thailand’s Ambassador-designate Phuchphop Mongkolnavin , President Nicușor Dan highlighted relations developed over more than five decades. Both sides expressed interest in strengthening economic cooperation through increased trade and investment and in diversifying sectoral cooperation, particularly in education, technology and cybersecurity . Côte d’Ivoire: agriculture, energy and strategic resources In his meeting with Côte d’Ivoire’s Ambassador-designate Yacouba Cissé , President Nicușor Dan expressed interest in intensifying political dialogue and expanding bilateral cooperation. The discussions focused on agriculture, energy, mineral resources and education , as well as opportunities to diversify cooperation in the port, oil and investment sectors. Panama: stronger ties with Central America During his meeting with Panama’s Ambassador-designate Javier Enrique Caraballo Salazar , President Nicușor Dan reaffirmed Romania’s commitment to developing relations with Central American countries. He expressed openness to deepening relations with Panama through increased trade and reciprocal investment. The two sides also discussed opportunities for cooperation in the economic, cultural and academic fields. Cambodia: trade, tourism and technology In talks with Cambodian Ambassador-designate Chea Chanboribo , President Nicușor Dan expressed appreciation for the friendly relations between the two countries and Romania’s interest in expanding cooperation in trade, tourism, education and technology . The two sides also highlighted their strong cooperation in multilateral frameworks, including the International Organisation of La Francophonie . President Nicușor Dan congratulated Cambodia on hosting the 20th Francophonie Summit in November and noted that Romania is running for the position of Secretary General of the organisation. Guatemala and El Salvador: expanding cooperation in Central America During his meeting with Guatemalan Ambassador-designate Gabriel Orellana Zabalza , President Nicușor Dan reaffirmed Romania’s openness to expanding bilateral trade and investment, including through the EU-CELAC cooperation framework . Education, agriculture, cybersecurity and technology were also identified as areas with potential for closer cooperation. In talks with El Salvador’s Ambassador-designate Kennedy Obed Reyes Lazo , the Romanian President confirmed Bucharest’s interest in strengthening relations with Central American countries and deepening traditional ties with El Salvador. The discussions included political dialogue, economic and trade relations, as well as cooperation in academia, IT, cybersecurity and research . Ghana: education, energy and digital cooperation Finally, during his meeting with Ghanaian Ambassador-designate Theresa Adjei-Mensah , President Nicușor Dan welcomed the level and positive dynamics of relations between Romania and Ghana. Both sides agreed on the importance of accelerating and diversifying bilateral cooperation, particularly in education, energy, cybersecurity, IT and institutional reform . A broad diplomatic agenda for Romania The meetings at Cotroceni Palace underline the breadth of Romania’s current diplomatic priorities, combining traditional economic and cultural partnerships with increasingly prominent issues of security, defence, energy resilience, connectivity and cybersecurity . From the Black Sea and NATO’s Eastern Flank to the Middle East, Asia, Africa and Latin America, President Nicușor Dan’s discussions with the newly appointed ambassadors reflected Romania’s interest in strengthening political dialogue while turning diplomatic relationships into concrete economic and strategic partnerships. The meetings also come at a time when Romania is seeking to consolidate its position as a key security and economic actor on NATO’s Eastern Flank while deepening cooperation with partners beyond Europe. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c34g.text: Figure caption, Moscow oil refinery seen on fire after Ukrainian drone attack By Jaroslav Lukiv Â and Â Dearbail Jordan Published 20 September 2026, 06:04 BST Updated 1 hour ago At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called an "unprecedented attack". An oil refinery was damaged and several homes were set ablaze. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine". Ukrainian officials meanwhile said eight people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday. Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs. A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured. An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Vorobyev added. Videos have emerged on social media appearing to show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC. Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged in "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election. Sunday is the third day of voting in an election that is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and which critics have dismissed as neither free, fair nor transparent. Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A building in the Moscow region early on Sunday, which Russian officials said had been hit by a Ukrainian drone strike Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed. It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Sautrday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko. He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital. In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said. Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so. Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India. The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5y.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, War in Sudan has led to the worst humanitarian crisis with more than 33 million people in need of assistance according to the WHO By Ondiro Oganga Published 1 hour ago The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine. In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production. "There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted. The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people. The statement , external was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website. It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger. "I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said. While the war in Sudan has led to what the World Health Organization has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, Roble said only 40% of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September. "Their meals come from the community kitchen, which doesn't really even have very long-term support because of funding cuts," Roble added. The joint statement warns that "the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000" without immediate action. The crisis is being exacerbated by what the signatories describe as systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El NiÃ±o, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of Sudan. "The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people," the statement says, urging them to lift all impediments to humanitarian assistance and allow full, safe, rapid and unimpeded access. In June, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a measure of the severity and magnitude of food crises, estimated that 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger. The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The incident coincided with an unidentified drone breaching Lithuanian airspace on Sunday morning, prompting Sinkevičius to convene an emergency meeting of the National Security Commission on Oct. 19 to examine debris, trace flight paths, and consider expanded statutory powers for neutralizing unmanned aircraft amid heightened Baltic vigilance against Russian hybrid sabotage. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 18, 2026, 1:46 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Lithuania’s Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius speaks during the Warsaw Security Forum in Warsaw, Poland, Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip An overnight arson attack targeting a Lithuanian logistics facility storing Starlink satellite communications equipment was thwarted by security measures, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius announced on Sunday, Oct. 18. Writing on Facebook, Sinkevičius confirmed that the attempted sabotage occurred shortly after midnight, but failed to inflict damage because national intelligence and security services had alerted the enterprise in advance. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Today after midnight, another incident occurred – an attempt was made to set fire to a Lithuanian company where Starlink communications equipment is stored,” Sinkevičius stated. “The security services had warned this company of prospective attacks, security had been reinforced, and the attempt was unsuccessful.” Advertisement National Security Commission convened over sabotage and drone intrusion Following the attempted arson, Sinkevičius announced that he is convening an emergency session of the National Security Commission on Monday, Oct. 19. The high-level security meeting will address the attempted facility attack alongside a separate aerial provocation detected early Sunday morning, when an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle breached Lithuanian sovereign airspace. “It is necessary to determine where the drone flew from and where radar systems first began tracking it,” the prime minister explained. “The findings of the services following their examination of the debris will also be critical. Furthermore, we will consider granting our services additional statutory powers to neutralize drones.” Other Topics of Interest Russia’s Rassvet Network Threatens Ukraine With Real-Time Strike Control Russia’s Rassvet satellite network could enable real-time control of Shahed drones and cruise missiles across Ukraine within six months. Sinkevičius emphasized that Lithuanian security agencies are monitoring the activities of hostile foreign states with heightened vigilance, coordinating protective protocols to shield critical infrastructure, civilian enterprises, and high-value supply chains. Expanding hybrid pressure across the Baltic littoral The thwarted attack in Lithuania coincides with an escalating campaign of state-sponsored hybrid warfare , physical sabotage, and airspace incursions directed against the Baltic states and Poland . Advertisement Allied intelligence agencies have repeatedly warned that Russian military intelligence (the GRU) and recruited proxies have intensified efforts to target European logistics hubs, supply warehouses, and communications nodes supporting Ukraine’s civil and military defense. On Friday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned following European Council consultations that Moscow could escalate hybrid attacks, sabotage operations , and border provocations against Poland and the Baltic nations before Christmas, highlighting transit corridors for fuel, food, and dual-use equipment as prime targets. Lithuanian security officials have noted that commercial satellite terminals, particularly Starlink equipment destined for government and defensive deployment, represent high-priority targets for hostile reconnaissance and interdiction given their vital role in sustaining frontline communications and emergency utilities. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.text: Figure caption, Burnt out and crushed vehicles were strew across the motorway in the aftermath of the crash By Hafsa Khalil Published 10 November 2026, 12:41 GMT Updated 6 hours ago Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said. Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries. Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported. Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway. Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident. The second crash, on the Sofia-bound carriageway, was likely also caused by the fog, with drivers also distracted by the first crash, BTA reported an official as saying. The Trakia motorway runs from west-to-east of Bulgaria, and connects the capital Sofia to the Black Sea coast. Road administration director Galin Kostov added that speeds were unsuitable for the conditions, which included wet road surfaces, and the motorway would remain closed until it had been cleared, BTA reported. Yambol regional governor Georgi Chalakov said reports first came in at 07:10 local time (05:10 GMT), with the injured taken by ambulance to hospitals in the Yambol, Sliven and Burgas regions. Chalakov told BTA rescue teams had to remove sections of the crash barrier to reach people. He added that the fog meant that helicopters could not be used in the evacuation efforts. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A drone captured the scene from above, just visible through the dense fog One witness who helped rescue a man from a burning vehicle blamed "very thick fog" for the pile-up. "I got out of the car, I ran forward and pulled that man out," the witness told Reuters news agency. Another told Reuters that "many, many people died". "As for me, there were four cars behind me - trucks - and I don't know how I got out or what happened, but in the end, thank God I'm still alive," that witness said. Radev - who had been hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen - cut short a news conference after learning of the incident and visited the scene.
